t: Self-Encrypting Drives: Encryption in the Hardware
title: Self-Encrypting Drives: Encryption in the Hardware
description: A self-encrypting drive encrypts every byte written to its media with a hardware AES engine — always on, transparent to the OS, with no performance penalty worth naming. The media encryption key never leaves the drive's crypto processor. Lose the drive, keep the data: without the key, the platters are noise.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: TCG Opal 2.0: The Management Standard
description: TCG Opal 2.0 is the Trusted Computing Group standard that manages SEDs: locking ranges (bands), admin/user authorities, and the protocols management software uses to lock, unlock, and erase. Opal is why drives from different makers answer the same commands. Samsung, Micron, and Seagate ship Opal drives.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: AES-256-XTS: The Media Cipher
description: SEDs encrypt media with AES-256 in XTS mode — the tweakable block cipher mode designed for storage, where each sector gets its own tweak so identical plaintexts encrypt differently per location. XTS is the storage industry's answer to ECB's pattern leaks. The mode matters as much as the key length.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: The Media Encryption Key (MEK)
description: The MEK is the drive's master secret, generated inside the drive at manufacture and never exposed — all media encryption flows from it. Authentication keys (passwords, tokens) wrap access to the MEK; the MEK itself never changes until crypto-erase. Protect the MEK and the data follows.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Crypto-Erase: Instant Sanitization
description: Crypto-erase destroys the MEK — regenerating it — which renders all data on the drive permanently unreadable in milliseconds, no overwrite passes needed. Decommissioning, repurposing, and emergency sanitization all use it. NIST SP 800-88 recognizes cryptographic erase as sanitization. Fast, final, and auditable.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Locking Ranges (Bands)
description: Opal bands partition the drive into independently lockable ranges — the OS band unlocked at boot, a data band requiring authentication. Multi-tenant and multi-level systems isolate data by band. Bands are the access-control lists of the drive.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Pre-Boot Authentication
description: Pre-boot authentication unlocks Opal bands before the OS loads — password, smart card, or TPM-sealed key — so the OS only ever sees decrypted media after authorization. Stolen laptop, powered off: the bands stay locked. PBA is the everyday face of SED security.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: PSID Revert: The Factory Reset
description: The PSID (physical secure ID printed on the drive label) authorizes a revert that crypto-erases the drive back to factory state — the recovery path when passwords are lost. Physical possession of the label equals ownership. Guard the label like a password.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: SEDs vs Software Encryption
description: SEDs encrypt in hardware at full media speed with zero CPU load and no OS dependence; software encryption (BitLocker/LUKS without HW assist) costs CPU and lives in the OS's trust domain. Best practice layers both: SED for media, software for defense in depth. Different layers, different failures.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Enterprise Management: Central Control
description: Enterprise SED management centralizes policies, key escrow, and remote lock/erase across fleets — lost laptop gets crypto-erased over the network before it can be attacked. Central visibility turns drives from liabilities into managed assets. Scale demands centralization.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: TCG Enterprise and Ruby SSCs
description: Beyond Opal, TCG defines Enterprise SSC (datacenter drives) and Ruby SSC (NVMe) — the same self-encryption concepts across SATA, SAS, and NVMe transports. The standard follows the interface. One management model, every drive type.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Validating SED Implementations
description: SED claims get validated: FIPS 140-3 for the crypto module, TCG certification for Opal compliance, and independent testing that locked bands actually stay locked. Marketing says 'encrypted'; validation proves it. Procurement should demand the paperwork.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Key Escrow and Recovery
description: Enterprise escrow stores recovery keys centrally so a forgotten password does not brick a drive — with strict access controls and audit on every escrow use. Escrow is the business continuity half of encryption. Uncontrolled escrow is a backdoor; controlled escrow is recovery.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: End-of-Life and Sanitization
description: Drive end-of-life follows NIST SP 800-88: crypto-erase for SEDs, with verification that the MEK was destroyed and data unrecoverable. Sanitization certificates document the chain of custody. Disposal without sanitization is a breach with a shipping label.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: The SED Security Picture
description: Ladder-top SED: hardware AES-XTS on all media, Opal-managed bands and authorities, crypto-erase sanitization, enterprise escrow and remote control. Fifteen rungs from a crypto chip to fleets of drives that stay dark when stolen.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.
